We quantified metatarsal and proximal phalangeal lengths across all five pedal rays in Gorilla, comparing western lowland gorillas (Gorilla gorilla gorilla), low- and high-elevation Grauer's gorillas (Gorilla beringei graueri), and two ecologically distinct mountain gorilla (Gorilla beringei beringei) populations: those of Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, Uganda, and the Virunga Massif (Volcanoes National Park, Rwanda). The Bwindi sample, assembled from individuals recovered by the Mountain Gorilla Skeletal Project between 2017 and 2025, represents the first substantial pedal dataset for this population. After separately scaling element lengths by estimated body mass and hindlimb length, Bwindi gorillas' third and fourth metatarsal lengths fell consistently between those of the more arboreal western lowland and highly terrestrial Virunga gorillas, while proximal phalangeal and hallux lengths varied little across populations. Additionally, Virunga gorillas showed longer second metatarsals compared to other populations, a feature we link to their strongly terrestrial locomotor habits. In comparing relative manual and pedal element lengths from the same individuals, metacarpals were relatively longer than metatarsals across all populations in rays 2-5, with this pattern reversed in the hallux; among these, only the second ray showed a significant interpopulation difference, with western lowland gorillas exhibiting relatively longer metacarpals than all other groups. Though interpopulation differences in the lengths of pedal elements were generally weaker than those found in the manual elements of the same individuals, these findings suggest that habitat-associated variation in foot morphology can be detected between populations of gorilla subspecies, underscoring the value of fine-grained, population-level skeletal comparisons for refining locomotor inference in the hominoid and hominin fossil record.

articles.title: Exercise-based rehabilitation interventions for kinesiophobia after total knee arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.authors: Hongbo Wen, Ting Zhang, Tingting Xie et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Affecting 21-35% of patients after total knee arthroplasty (TKA), kinesiophobia critically impedes postoperative rehabilitation. Whether exercise-based interventions reduce kinesiophobia more effectively than routine postoperative rehabilitation remains unclear. METHODS: We systematically searched 11 databases from inception to July 11, 2026, for RCTs comparing exercise-based rehabilitation with routine postoperative rehabilitation in adults undergoing primary TKA. The primary outcome was kinesiophobia. Secondary outcomes included knee function, pain, balance, mobilization time, and adherence. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using RevMan 5.4. Certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. RESULTS: Eleven RCTs (N = 1,096) were included. Exercise-based rehabilitation was associated with a reduction in kinesiophobia (SMD = - 1.22, 95% CI [- 1.72, - 0.72]; I2 = 93%; low certainty) and improvements in knee function (SMD = 1.19, 95% CI [0.67, 1.71]; I2 = 93%; low certainty). For pain, the ≤ 4-week pooled estimate (SMD = - 1.09, 95% CI [- 2.03, - 0.14]; I2 = 94%) was not interpretable due to extreme heterogeneity and was not robust: after exclusion of the single acute in-hospital trial, the confidence interval crossed zero (SMD = - 1.09, 95% CI [- 2.28, 0.09]). Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses otherwise supported the directional conclusions for kinesiophobia and knee function, although effect sizes were unstable and certainty remained low. CONCLUSION: Low-certainty evidence suggests that exercise-based rehabilitation may be associated with reductions in kinesiophobia at ≤ 4 weeks and an interpretable 12-week improvement in knee function after TKA; the ≤ 4-week and ≥ 24-week functional subgroup estimates were not interpretable because of extreme heterogeneity, and the early pain signal was possible but non-robust. Effect sizes should be interpreted with caution due to substantial heterogeneity, risk of bias, and sensitivity to outlying studies. Well-designed, multicenter RCTs with rigorous blinding and standardized protocols are urgently needed.

articles.title: Dietary Supplement Use and Beliefs Among Athletes at the 2025 Canada Games.
articles.journal: Applied physiology, nutrition, and metabolism = Physiologie appliquee, nutrition et metabolisme
articles.authors: Jana Daher, Adriah Kate Sahajpal, Vijay Sahajpal et al.
articles.abstract: Dietary supplement use is widespread among athletes; however, limited data exist regarding supplement use and beliefs among Canadian youth athletes. This cross-sectional online study aimed to examine dietary supplement use and related beliefs among athletes competing at the 2025 Canada Games in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador. A total of 473 respondents participated in the survey. Of the 473 participants, 385 completed responses to the dietary supplement (DS) questions. Among participants who reported their sex, 125 were male and 189 were female. Overall, 36% of participants reported current dietary supplement use. Supplement use was significantly higher among males than females (47% vs. 23%, p < .001) and increased with age (p = .001). The most commonly reported supplements were protein powder (49%), sports drinks (46%), and creatine (45%). Primary reasons for use included maintaining good health (76%), increasing energy (54%), and promoting recovery (50%). Coaches (50%) and healthcare professionals (49%) were the most frequently reported information sources. Supplement users demonstrated significantly stronger positive beliefs regarding benefits of dietary supplements compared with non-users (all p < .001). Ordinal logistic regression showed that supplement users had greater odds of stronger agreement that supplements improve performance (OR = 5.50, 95% CI: 3.31-9.13, p < .001). These findings highlight the use of dietary supplements among Canadian youth athletes and support the need for targeted nutrition education to promote informed decision-making.

articles.title: Functional Adaptations for Load-Bearing in a Dermal Bone: The Pectoral Fin Spine of the Russian Sturgeon (Huso Gueldenstaedtii).
articles.authors: Esteban Marroquín-Arroyave, Joshua Milgram
articles.abstract: Dermal bone, which forms a variety of skeletal structures and persists in a wide range of extant vertebrates, evolved prior to endochondral bone which forms all mammalian load-bearing long bones. Sturgeons (Acipenseriformes) are an early-diverging extant lineage of actinopterygians that retain prominent post-cranial dermal skeletal elements. They retain a long robust spine at the leading edge of the pectoral fin, called the pectoral fin spines (PFS). PFS are bone elements that are present in many extinct and extant species of non-tetrapod jawed fish. In this study, we characterize the structure (light, polarized, micro-computed tomography and scanning electron microscopy), composition (FTIR, TGA, BMD), and mechanical properties (3-point bending and microindentation) of the PFS of the Russian sturgeon (Huso gueldenstaedtii). The microstructure of the PFS is highly organized as it is formed by dermal osteonal bone and parallel fibered bone. Its microarchitecture, along with high material toughness, anisotropy, and substantial ash content, enables the PFS to bear loads and function in both locomotion and protection. In addition, we show an interconnected network of neurovascular canals and ornamentations, features also found in PFS of other non-tetrapod jawed fish. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that dermal bone can form structurally organized, mechanically competent load-bearing elements and provide new insights into PFSs in ray-finned fish.

articles.title: The Fibular Artery Communicating Branch and Fibular Artery Dominance: An Anatomical Hazard for Posterior Approaches to the Ankle.
articles.authors: Annabelle Johnston McCarter, Chijioke Orji, Craig Wyatt et al.
articles.abstract: Open reduction of posterior malleolar fractures (PMFs) increasingly employs direct posterior approaches. The posterolateral and posteromedial approaches both develop the deep posterior compartment in the plane between the fibular and posterior tibial arteries, placing the fibular artery communicating branch (FACB) within the operative field; inadvertent injury to this branch has been associated with limb-threatening ischemia. This study quantified the prevalence of the FACB and of fibular artery dominance (FAD), a configuration in which the fibular artery provides the principal distal supply because the posterior tibial artery is atretic or absent, and considered the implications for surgical approach selection. In a single-center cross-sectional study, 916 consecutive lower-limb computed tomography angiograms performed over 1 year were screened; 726 met the inclusion criteria and were assessed by trained reviewers for the FACB, FAD, laterality and clinical indication. An FACB was identified in 280 patients (38.6%, 95% CI 35.1-42.2). Its prevalence varied with clinical indication (χ2 = 33.67, p < 0.001), being highest in peripheral vascular disease (45.1%) and lowest in other vascular referrals (16.4%). FAD occurred exclusively in FACB-positive limbs, in 28 patients (10.0% of FACB-positive limbs; 3.9% of the whole cohort, 95% CI 2.7-5.5), and its distribution did not differ by indication (Freeman-Halton exact p = 0.81). Because the FACB lies within the field of the posterolateral and posteromedial approaches but posterior and lateral to the medial-posteromedial (MPM) approach, the MPM approach avoids the at-risk plane. These findings support anatomically informed approach selection and caution when a posterolateral or posteromedial approach is planned, particularly in patients with peripheral vascular disease.

articles.title: Turkish Research Dietitians Prioritize Strengthening Traditional Methods Before Digital Transition: A Qualitative Study.
articles.authors: Merve Guney-Coskun, Michelle Weech, Rosalind Fallaize et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dietary assessment underpins nutrition research and practice. Food Frequency Questionnaires (FFQs) are used in epidemiology yet have limitations. Digital technologies are reshaping dietary assessment, with potential to improve scalability and standardization. Understanding how dietitians appraise traditional and emerging approaches is critical for guiding context-appropriate innovation. OBJECTIVE: This study explored research-focused Turkish dietitians' perspectives on (i) the strengths and limitations of FFQs, (ii) opportunities and barriers in transitioning to web-based FFQs, and (iii) the potential and challenges of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI) and biosensors, in dietary assessment, with Türkiye-specific considerations where relevant. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with ten PhD-qualified, research-focused dietitians in Türkiye, purposively sampled for dietary assessment expertise. Interviews were conducted online, transcribed, and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Sample size was guided by thematic saturation; recruitment continued until no substantively new themes emerged across successive interviews. RESULTS: Participants valued FFQs as scalable tools for capturing habitual intake but noted limits in person-level detail, portion accuracy, and recall reliability. Culturally adapted food lists and portion imagery were perceived as priorities to improve validity. Web-based FFQs were viewed as a credible evolution offering efficiency and visual supports, though concerns centered on digital literacy, device access, and user guidance. Emerging tools such as AI-assisted image capture and wearable biosensors were considered promising for reducing memory bias and improving objectivity, but adoption was tempered by concerns over cost, usability, cultural fit, privacy, and governance. CONCLUSIONS: The perspectives of the Turkish research-focused dietitians interviewed in this study point to a staged pathway for innovation: first to strengthen FFQ content with cultural adaptation and visual supports; then digitize with safeguards for accessibility and data integrity; and finally pilot advanced technologies cautiously, under robust validation and ethical oversight. This phased approach could offer an acceptable pathway to modernizing dietary assessment while safeguarding credibility and equity.

articles.title: Maximum Deceleration Is Related to Players' Ability to Repeat High-Intensity Decelerations in a Match in Female Professional Soccer Players.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: David Martínez-Hernández, Paul A Jones, José M Oliva-Lozano et al.
articles.abstract: Martínez-Hernández, D, Jones, PA, Oliva-Lozano, JM, and Harper, DJ. Maximum deceleration is related to players' ability to repeat high-intensity decelerations in a match in female professional soccer players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was twofold; First, to investigate positional differences in high-intensity decelerations (HID; < -3 m·s-2) and very high-intensity decelerations (VHID; < -4 m·s-2) in elite female soccer players. Second, to examine relationships between maximum deceleration (DMax) and the frequency of HID and VHID throughout competitive match play, reflecting players' capacity to perform these actions repeatedly. Twenty-four professional female outfield players (189 match files) from an English Women's Superleague club were tracked across 27 matches using 10-Hz Global Positioning System devices. Differences in deceleration metrics (DMax, HID, VHID) across positions were analyzed using 1-way analysis of variance and Bonferroni post hoc tests. Pearson's correlations assessed relationships between DMax, HID, and VHID across playing positions. Significant positional differences were observed. Central defenders had the lowest DMax and performed fewer HID and VHID actions than other positions, whereas central midfielder recorded the highest HID values. Maximum deceleration showed moderate-to-large correlations with HID (r = 0.35) and VHID (r = 0.52). Positional and individual variations influenced the strength of these relationships. This study provides novel evidence that maximal deceleration capacity is an important neuromuscular performance quality that distinguishes playing positions in elite women's soccer, with moderate-to-large associations with the ability to perform repeated HID and VHID supporting its relevance to match performance, particularly at higher intensities. These findings suggest that DMax may be an important quality to target through training, with potential implications for repeated deceleration performance. Practitioners should implement position-specific assessments and interventions to optimize deceleration capacity, especially as modern game demands continue to evolve.

articles.title: Intense unimanual contractions increase muscle excitation and local metabolic activity in the resting contralateral forearm.
articles.authors: Lee J Hinkle, Britton C Scheuermann, Carl J Ade et al.
articles.abstract: Intense unilateral muscle contractions evoke measurable activity within the contralateral neuroaxis, which can be detected with surface electromyographic activity in the resting homologous muscle. Physiological mirror activity (PMA), the unintentional increase in contralateral muscle excitation, has been implicated in cross-limb interactions and adaptations. Despite longstanding observations of PMA, it remains unknown whether this low-level muscle excitation influences local muscle metabolism. We addressed this question using a vascular occlusion test in 10 healthy adults. Surface electromyography and near-infrared spectroscopy-derived measures of tissue oxygen saturation and muscle oxygen consumption ( m V . O 2 ) were obtained from the resting left forearm during vascular occlusion at rest and during fatiguing unimanual contractions. PMA in the contralateral resting arm was greater during fatiguing unimanual contractions than during rest (mean difference: 8.9%, 95% CI: 4.1 to 13.8). This increase was accompanied by a steeper rate of tissue oxygen desaturation (mean difference: -0.132% s- 1, 95% CI: -0.227 to -0.037) and greater m V . O 2 (mean difference: 0.188 mL O2 min- 1 100 g- 1, 95% CI: 0.057 to 0.320). Greater PMA was associated with both a faster rate of oxygen desaturation (r = -0.85, 95% CI: -0.96 to -0.46) and greater m V . O 2 (r = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.28 to 0.94). These findings provide the first evidence that PMA is accompanied by increased local metabolic demand, consistent with a coupling between unintentional muscle excitation and oxygen extraction in the resting limb.

articles.title: Rethinking the application and adoption of NOVA classification in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs): a Southeast Asian food systems perspective.
articles.authors: C Jeyakumar Henry, M Aman Wirakartakusumah, E-Siong Tee et al.
articles.abstract: Ultra-processed foods have increasingly been associated with chronic disease risk in global analyses. The NOVA classification is positioned to influence dietary guidelines, food manufacturing, and public health policy worldwide. This paper argues that the NOVA classification, when applied without contextual adaptation, may be inappropriate for Southeast Asian food systems. It could misdirect policy interventions aimed at addressing both the double burden of under- and overnutrition. By labelling foods as UPFs, NOVA may obscure the essential role that certain processed foods play in improving nutritional outcomes and advancing public health. An overemphasis on the negative impact of processed and ultra-processed foods risks oversimplifying complex dietary patterns in Asia and other LMICs. It may also undermine nutritional gains achieved over the past four decades.

articles.title: Hydroxyproline Enhances Branched-Chain Amino Acid Effects on Lifespan and Healthspan in Caenorhabditis elegans.
articles.authors: Linggao Liu, Ruiyun Wu, Ziwu Gao et al.
articles.abstract: Food-derived protein hydrolysates frequently contain both collagen-associated hydroxyproline (Hyp) and branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), but the biological consequences of their combination remain unclear. This study tested whether Hyp changes the effects of leucine (Leu), isoleucine (Ile), and valine (Val) on lifespan and healthspan-related phenotypes in Caenorhabditis elegans and whether these treatment effects are accompanied by coordinated microbial and metabolic remodeling. Amino acid concentrations that did not strongly disrupt bacterial food clearance were selected for lifespan, stress-resistance, motility, muscle-integrity, biochemical, microbiome, metabolomic, and transcriptomic analyses. Hyp+BCAA combinations improved lifespan- and healthspan-related phenotypes in a BCAA- and dose-dependent manner. The strongest combined treatments enhanced resistance to thermal and oxidative stress, preserved age-associated motility and muscle structure, reduced oxidative and lipofuscin-associated markers, and increased ATP-related readouts. Multi-omics profiling showed that these direct treatment effects were accompanied by distinct C. elegans-associated microbiota signatures, altered NAD precursor-related metabolites including nicotinic acid ribonucleoside (NaR), and a Leu+Hyp transcriptional response enriched for energy metabolism, proteostasis, and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Integrated microbiome-metabolome analysis identified a positive association between Rhodococcus abundance and NaR levels. These findings demonstrate that, under the tested culture conditions, Hyp+BCAA exposure improves longevity-related phenotypes and identifies microbial composition, NAD precursor metabolism, and host energy homeostasis as candidate, testable mediators.

articles.title: Maternal Mannan-Oligosaccharide improves intestinal resilience of weanling pigs via enhancing milk-mediated immune transfer.
articles.authors: Siyu Yuan, Zhenting He, Ronghua Yao et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Maternal nutrition during late gestation and lactation influences milk composition and early-life intestinal development. Whether maternal mannan-oligosaccharide (MOS) supplementation enhances offspring resilience during weaning remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: The effects of maternal MOS supplementation on sow physiology, milk quality, offspring growth, and intestinal responses to an acute inflammatory challenge were evaluated. METHODS: Sixty sows received a control diet or 800 mg MOS/kg diet from gestation day 85 to lactation day 21 (n = 30/group). Reproductive outcomes (litter size, birth weight, subsequent estrus, insemination, conception, and farrowing) and litter outcomes (survival, daily gain, and weaning weight at 21 d) were recorded. Sow feces were collected on gestation day 109 for microbiota analysis, plasma and colostrum at farrowing and milk on lactation day 14 for antioxidant, inflammatory, nutrient, and immunoglobulin analyses, as applicable. At weaning, 24 piglets from 12 litters received saline or lipopolysaccharide (LPS; 100 μg/kg). Plasma and intestinal tissues were collected 6 h later for antioxidant, morphology, barrier, and inflammation measurements. Mixed models assessed maternal diet and, in piglets, maternal diet × LPS, with litter accounted for. RESULTS: Compared with controls, MOS increased sow lactation feed intake (5.68 vs 5.21 kg/d; P = 0.036), piglet daily gain (224.22 vs 195.35 g/d; P < 0.001), and weaning weight (6.67 vs 5.91 kg; P < 0.001). Colostral fat and IgA were 5.26% vs 3.80% and 5.37 vs 3.00 mg/mL, respectively; day-14 milk fat and IgA were 7.72% vs 5.19% and 0.43 vs 0.19 mg/mL (all P < 0.05). Relative to LPS-challenged controls, maternal MOS increased jejunal occludin protein (0.78 vs 0.44, normalized to β-actin) and decreased jejunal IL-1β (146.31 vs 169.77 pg/mL; both P < 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Maternal MOS supplementation improved milk-mediated nutritional and immune transfer and enhanced intestinal resilience of offspring during weaning-associated inflammatory stress in piglets.

articles.title: The ascending aorta and vascular profile in recreational masters runners: a cross-sectional study.
articles.authors: Wioletta Sacharczuk, Rafał Dankowski, Dagmara Tritt et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Endurance exercise remodels the large arteries, but whether a recreational training dose is sufficient to induce such remodelling is unclear. Masters recreational runners over 40 years are under-represented in this research. We compared the ascending aortic diameter and vascular profile of these runners with sedentary controls of similar age. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 42 masters recreational runners (at least 20 km per week for at least one year) and 27 sedentary controls, all over 40 years, free of cardiovascular disease and without bicuspid aortic valve or connective tissue disorder. We measured the ascending aortic diameter and left ventricular function by transthoracic echocardiography, and brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity (baPWV) and the ankle-brachial index (ABI) by oscillometry. Circulating collagen-turnover markers (CTX-I, MMP-2) were assayed. The aortic diameter was compared between groups by regression. RESULTS: The ascending aorta was wider in runners (3.25 vs. 2.90 cm; p = 0.001; Cliff's delta 0.45). The difference persisted after adjustment for age, sex and height (beta 0.31 cm; p = 0.001) and in sensitivity analyses. No aortic diameter reached 4.0 cm; all remained within normal limits. The ABI was higher in runners (1.07 vs. 1.03; p = 0.007), and baPWV did not differ (p = 0.069); both stayed within normal limits. CTX-I and MMP-2 did not differ, and left ventricular function was preserved. CONCLUSION: These findings are consistent with modest, exercise-associated aortic remodelling rather than overt aortopathy in recreational masters runners over 40 years.

articles.title: Blood lactate concentrations are associated with markers of metabolic dysfunction during late pregnancy.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism
articles.authors: Regis C Pearson, Destiny P Hamilton, Nicholas T Broskey et al.
articles.abstract: The ability to detect metabolic dysfunction during pregnancy can impact the health of mother and infant(s). Lactate may serve as a biomarker to predict metabolic dysfunction risk. The purpose of this study was to determine if fasting or postprandial blood lactate concentrations were related to established markers of metabolic dysfunction during late pregnancy. Overnight fasted healthy women between 32-38 weeks gestation underwent a high-fat meal test. Fasted and postprandial (1h, 2h, and 4h) venous blood glucose, insulin, and lactate were collected. Fasted and postprandial (2h and 4h) respiratory exchange ratios (RERs) were assessed by indirect calorimetry. HOMA-IR and Matsuda indexes were calculated. Participants were categorized into lean (18.5-24.9 kg/m2), overweight (25.0-29.9 kg/m2), or obese (≥30.0 kg/m2) based on pre-pregnancy body mass index. To determine the impact that weight status may have on postprandial lactate concentrations, a repeated-measures analysis of variance was performed on log-transformed data. Spearman's rank-order correlation coefficients were used to assess associations between outcome variables. 52 participants were included in the analysis (lean, n = 29; overweight, n = 11; obese, n = 12). Postprandial lactate was higher in women with obesity compared to women who were lean (1h, p = 0.024; 2h, p = 0.025; 4h, p = 0.010). Among all women, higher lactate area under the curve (AUC) was associated with higher insulin AUC, higher HOMA-IR index, lower Matsuda index, and higher RER AUC (p ≤ 0.003). These findings suggest that postprandially elevated lactate may serve as a useful biomarker for identifying metabolic dysfunction during pregnancy.

articles.title: How to Implement a Ketogenic Diet Therapy in Developing Countries: Colombian Consensus on Ketogenic Diet Therapy Use in the Management of Adults with Drug-Resistant Epilepsy.
articles.authors: Jean Paul Vergara-Aguilar, Angélica Lizcano, Adriana Martinez-Perez et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Drug-resistant epilepsy affects up to one-third of patients with epilepsy and is associated with higher morbidity, mortality, trauma events, psychosocial challenges, and decline in quality of life. In Latin America, disease burden is high and access to advanced therapies remains limited. Ketogenic Diet Therapy (KDT) has been shown to be beneficial in adults, but its implementation requires standardized protocols and experienced multidisciplinary teams. This study aimed to develop practical, evidence-based recommendations to guide the indication, implementation, and follow-up of KDT in adults with drug-resistant epilepsy through expert consensus in Colombia. METHODS: A modified version of the Nominal Group Technique was used to develop, discuss, and vote on management concepts. Clinical questions were structured using the PICO framework. Literature searches were conducted in PubMed and EMBASE for articles published since 2015, and the evidence was integrated with the experience of a multidisciplinary expert panel. RESULTS: Twelve recommendations were issued, covering commercial formulas, induction and follow-up protocols, individualized dietary interventions, safety, diagnostic support, nutritional supplementation, and drug-diet interactions. The consensus highlights the need for interdisciplinary teams, structured education, early adherence strategies, and close follow-up, and the role of enteral emergency formulas in intensive care settings. CONCLUSIONS: Evidence around KDT shows it can be implemented safely as an adjunctive treatment for adults with drug-resistant epilepsy and is reasonable to consider following the failure of two adequate antiseizure medications. Structured implementation may reduce seizure frequency, improve quality of life, and reduce the pharmacological burden. Multicenter prospective studies are needed to further assess efficacy, safety, and resource utilization. These recommendations contribute to closing the gap between evidence and clinical practice.

articles.title: Surgical Profiles of Elite Female Athletes and Their Association with Long-Term Musculoskeletal Health: Findings from the Women's Soccer Health Study.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Kai-Lun Law, Polly de Mille, Heidi Prather et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To describe the career and post-career surgeries in female elite-level soccer players and evaluate their association with long-term musculoskeletal health. STUDY DESIGN: This is a cross-sectional study. METHODS: Surgical data (the number and type of surgeries during and after the career) from an anonymous online survey was obtained from a previously published cohort of 560 retired elite women's soccer players. Correlation coefficients were used to evaluate the relationship between the number of surgeries and physical activity levels (UCLA activity scale), joint function (SANE), and physical and mental health (PROMIS-10), which were all collected on the same survey. RESULTS: The average number of career surgeries was 1 (SD=1.6), and the average number of post-career surgeries was 0.5 (SD=1). The most common career surgery sites for women's soccer players were knee (39%), foot/ankle (12%), and leg (4%). The most common knee procedures involved ligament reconstruction, primarily of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), followed by meniscus and cartilage surgery. The most frequent post-career surgery sites were knee (24.0%), foot/ankle (5.1%), and leg (3.2%). Knee ligament and meniscus surgeries were equally reported. More career and post-career surgeries were associated with lower SANE knee scores (p<0.001). Lower SANE knee scores (p=0.017) were associated with lower UCLA activity levels. CONCLUSIONS: The locations of career and post-career surgeries were similar, suggesting a possible association with long-term musculoskeletal impairment, particularly to the knee, in a cohort of mostly White collegiate former players. Having more soccer-related surgeries was associated with reduced joint function and activity levels after retirement, though the correlations were weak or moderate. These findings suggest the need for the development of preventive interventions that address the specific needs of female athletes, implementation of injury prevention programs and strategies to maximize adherence, and long-term musculoskeletal assessments of players after retirement.

articles.title: An Acute Alcoholic Beer Dose Impaired Exercise Performance: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Crossover Trial.
articles.journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism
articles.authors: Felipe De Russi de Lima, Vitor de Salles Painelli, Raul Canestri et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: We investigated whether a small dose of alcoholic beer ingested before a running exercise bout impaired performance and changed psychophysiological responses to exercise. METHODS: After three sessions of familiarizations, 16 healthy and physically active men (25.8 ± 5.1 years, 175.0 ± 5.4 cm, and 76 ± 6.5 kg) performed a 30-min running time trial in a double-blind and placebo-controlled crossover design, after ingesting either beer (alcohol 4.8% v/v; 0.3 g/kg) or nonalcoholic beer (placebo). Performance, cardiopulmonary (oxygen consumption, ventilation, respiratory exchange ratio, and heart rate), and perceptual (perceived exertion, affect, and motivation) variables were assessed throughout the trial and averaged every 5 min during exercise. Running economy was assessed during steady-state running at 8 km/hr. The data were analyzed through t tests and repeated-measures mixed models (p < .05). RESULTS: The ingestion of beer significantly decreased the average speed by 4.7% (p = .04; d = 0.21) and total distance covered by 4.3% (p = .007; d = 0.26) when compared with placebo. The ingestion of beer also impaired the running economy by 1.1% (p = .01; d = 0.39) and increased respiratory exchange ratio throughout the exercise bout (p = .004, d = 1.07). No beer-by-time interaction effects were detected in cardiopulmonary outcomes (p > .05). CONCLUSIONS: A small dose of alcoholic beer reduced the exercise capacity of healthy individuals, likely due to an impairment in running economy.

articles.title: Not Just Faster Horses: Telerehabilitation as a Necessary Evolution in Physical Therapy.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: Miguel Farraj, Julien Lebleu, Bruno Bonnechère et al.
articles.abstract: SYNOPSIS: This editorial draws an analogy between the transition from "faster horses" to automobiles and the digital transition facing musculoskeletal physical therapy. Musculoskeletal rehabilitation has long emphasized face-to-face sessions; digital solutions such as telerehabilitation have often been perceived as alternatives to conventional care. However, increasing rehabilitation demands, persistent gaps between sessions, and the need for long-term patient support highlight the importance of rethinking how physical therapists deliver care. We argue that telerehabilitation should not replace physical therapists but rather extend their role through facilitating continuous monitoring, communication, education, and patient engagement. Successful implementation requires more than simply adopting new technologies-it requires clinicians to develop new skills, adapt professional habits, and integrate digital tools while preserving therapeutic relationships and patient-centered care. Just as innovation required moving beyond faster horses, the future of musculoskeletal physical therapy may depend on embracing new models of care rather than simply iterating on traditional approaches. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):624-626. Epub 28 Aug 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14510.

articles.title: Hematological and biochemical responses to three doses of caffeine during the CrossFit® workout: a randomized, double-blind, crossover trial.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Natalia Główka, Tomasz Podgórski, Jakub Malik et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: This study investigated the effects of three doses of caffeine (CAF) on hematological and biochemical responses during the CrossFit® workout, a protocol known to induce significant physiological fluctuations. METHODS: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo (PLA)-controlled crossover trial, 26 moderately trained CrossFit® athletes received acute doses of 3, 6, or 9 mgCAF/kgbody mass (BM), or a PLA, 70 min before a 17-min CrossFit® workout. RESULTS: While exercise was the predominant driver of hematological changes, with no CAF-specific modulation of blood cell indices, significant treatment × time point interactions were observed solely for glucose concentration. Specifically, MEDIUM (6 mgCAF/kgBM) and HIGH (9 mgCAF/kgBM) CAF doses produced significantly greater post-exercise glucose elevations compared to baseline and PLA visits. Phosphates concentrations increased over time, particularly post-exercise, with no treatment effect retained after excluding baseline visit in the sensitivity analysis. Calcium level dynamics were influenced by temporal factors rather than CAF, and magnesium concentration remained stable. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that acute CAF ingestion selectively influences post-exercise glucose responses during the CrossFit® workout, whereas hematological variables and most biochemical markers remain unaffected. Significant post-exercise glucose elevations were observed following the 6 and 9 mgCAF/kgBM conditions compared with baseline and PLA visits, while serum mineral concentrations remained largely stable across treatments. CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTRATION: NCT03822663.

articles.title: The So-Called "Vastus Lateralis Obliquus" is the Most Distal Part of the Vastus Intermedius.
articles.authors: Takafumi Ono, Mio Imai, Yuto Kawasaki et al.
articles.abstract: The vastus lateralis (VL) has long been described as comprising a longitudinal part (vastus lateralis longus, VLL) and an oblique part (vastus lateralis obliquus, VLO), the latter inserting onto the superolateral border of the patella and traditionally regarded as a component of the VL that stabilizes the patella laterally. However, the anatomical relationship between the VLO and the remainder of the VL has never been rigorously defined, and electromyographic studies have independently regarded the muscle belly emerging at the distolateral thigh as the "superficial region of the vastus intermedius (VI)." To address this discrepancy, we re-examined the structure and innervation of the VLO in five thighs from five embalmed cadavers by gross dissection. The belly conventionally identified as the VLO was present in all specimens and inserted onto the superolateral patella. When the VLL was reflected, this belly was continuous with the VI, which arose broadly from the anterior surface of the femoral shaft; thus, the VLO was the most distal portion of the VI protruding lateral to the lateral border of the VL. Consistently, this region was supplied by the terminal twigs of the lateral branch of the VI (femoral nerve), whereas the branch to the VL did not reach it. We conclude that the so-called VLO is not part of the VL but the distal part of the VI. This reinterpretation reconciles the anatomical convention with electromyographic findings and has implications for anatomical nomenclature, interpretation of VI surface electromyography, and understanding the traction source in painful bipartite patella.

articles.title: Transient gait instability during the initial phase of the 6-minute walk test in people with stroke: A nonlinear analysis using inertial measurement units.
articles.authors: Yasuhiro Inui, Yusaku Takamura, Shu Morioka
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: In people with stroke (PwS), reduced gait speed and trunk acceleration changes in the latter half of the 6-minute walk test (6MWT) have been reported as fatigue-related, but temporal changes in motor control remain understudied. Clinicians often observe instability immediately after gait onset, yet quantitative evidence is scarce. This study used inertial measurement units (IMUs) and nonlinear analysis to examine fatigue-related changes and post-onset instability during the 6MWT in PwS. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 19 PwS and 19 age-matched controls completed the 6MWT wearing IMUs at the L5 vertebra and both ankles. Spatiotemporal parameters and stability indices (root mean square, harmonic ratio, sample entropy, short-term Lyapunov exponent [sLE]) were calculated. Linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) analyzed the 6-minute period both continuously and by comparing an initial phase (first 60 s) with the subsequent phase. Bayesian and sensitivity analyses were also performed. RESULTS: Continuous-time LMMs showed reduced cadence and increased double-support ratio in PwS. Among stability indices, only mediolateral sLE (sLE-ML) showed a significant group × phase interaction: increasing in the initial phase in PwS but not in controls. Bayesian and sensitivity analyses confirmed this finding was robust and specific to the 60-second cutoff. Initial-phase sLE-ML correlated negatively with Fugl-Meyer lower-extremity scores. CONCLUSIONS: PwS showed fatigue-related gait changes during the 6MWT, while mediolateral local dynamic stability transiently declined during the first 60 s before stabilizing. This instability was associated with motor paralysis, suggesting trunk IMU-based sLE-ML may reveal motor control deficits not captured by walking distance or speed.

articles.title: Left anterior laryngeal loop of the common carotid artery in a cluster of bilateral cervicothoracic vascular variants: a case report.
articles.authors: Viviana Dincă, Adelina Maria Jianu, Mugurel Constantin Rusu
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The common carotid artery (CCA) normally ascends in the carotid sheath, posterolateral to the larynx and trachea. Anterior or pretracheal CCA courses are rare and have been described mainly on the right, usually in relation to a high-riding brachiocephalic trunk (BCT) or another arch-level anomaly. We report a CTA case with a common-origin left CCA-BCT trunk, a high-riding BCT and bilateral carotid redundancy, including a left anterior laryngeal CCA loop. METHODS: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the aortic arch and bilateral carotid systems was reviewed using multiplanar reformatting and three-dimensional volume-rendered reconstruction. Vessel loops, branching points and relationships to the hyoid-laryngeal framework, thyroid gland and adjacent skeletal landmarks were recorded. RESULTS: CTA showed a common-origin left CCA-BCT trunk with a high-riding BCT measuring 3.27 cm. The right CCA formed a 1.79 cm lateral loop and bifurcated posterolateral to the hyoid-laryngeal framework; the right external carotid artery (ECA) gave rise to a linguofacial trunk and then formed a retromandibular loop. The left CCA formed a 2.15 cm intramediastinal loop and a 1.75 cm anterior laryngeal loop. The left superior thyroid artery arose directly from the CCA. The left ECA showed independent branching and a retromandibular loop. Tortuosity indices ranged from 33.1% to 92.7%; all segments were tortuous and the right internal carotid artery additionally formed a kink (apex angle 87.3°). CONCLUSION: This case documents a rare left anterior laryngeal CCA loop in association with bilateral carotid and external carotid branching variants. The left-sided anterior loop is the main surgical finding because it brings a major cervical artery close to the anterior laryngeal operative field. Recognition of this pattern is relevant before front-of-neck airway access, thyroid surgery, laryngotracheal surgery and central neck procedures.

articles.title: A Systematic Review of Food Swap Interventions Used in Grocery Store Settings.
articles.authors: Helena Bentil, Edward Hillier, Oliver Huse et al.
articles.abstract: CONTEXT: Food swap interventions provide an approach to influence consumer food choices. However, evidence on their design and effectiveness has not yet been synthesized. OBJECTIVE: This review systematically synthesized the literature on food swap interventions in grocery settings by addressing the following questions: (1) What were the key characteristics of the food swap interventions examined in the literature, and what was their intended purpose? (2) Have food swap interventions been effective in changing behavior? DATA SOURCES, EXTRACTION, AND ANALYSIS: A search of MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science up to January 23, 2025, was conducted to identify food swap intervention trials in grocery settings, with no limits on language or publication year. Covidence was used to screen titles, abstracts, and full-text articles in duplicate. Data were synthesized narratively. RESULTS: Eleven studies, published during 2006-2024, were included in the review. One intervention was implemented in a real grocery store, 3 in real online supermarkets, and 7 in simulated online supermarkets. Most included studies targeted adults with primary or partial responsibility for their household grocery shopping. All the swaps offered healthier alternatives to selected products. Outcomes examined included shopping basket item healthiness, energy content, saturated fatty acid (SFA) content, salt density, and sodium and sugar content. All but 1 study noted evidence that the studied interventions can change behavior. Two studies found significant improvements in overall nutritional quality. Salt/sodium reductions were seen in 2 studies, while reductions in sugar content were seen in 1 study but not in another study. Studies also demonstrated significant reductions in purchased energy content/density, and SFA. CONCLUSION: A range of food swap interventions have been studied, and most of those identified have been found to be effective in improving the healthiness of food purchases. No studies explored the potential of swap interventions to promote sustainable food choices, which could be a topic of future research. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO registration No. [CRD42024539803].

articles.title: Impact of minimally processed versus milled whole grains on glycaemic control in type 2 diabetes: A 12-week randomised trial.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Andrew N Reynolds, Fiona Hood, Ella Iosua et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Whole grains are widely promoted within a healthy diet, with dietary advice encouraging the replacement of refined grains with whole grains. However, data from small trials indicates that milling or processing whole grains may influence the glycaemic response. OBJECTIVE: To identify if clinically relevant HbA1c differs with processed (milled) or less processed (unmilled) whole grain intakes in type 2 diabetes management. METHODS: We conducted a 12-week randomised parallel trial in adults with type 2 diabetes. Participants received free and delivered whole grain foods that differed in degree of processing. Each intervention was of four foods from whole grain wheat, rice, and oats, in sufficient amounts (4.5-9kg per fortnight) to accommodate family size. Participants were advised to replace the grain foods they normally consumed with the provided products. The primary outcome was glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c). All analyses were performed using an intention-to-treat approach, with outcome variables investigated using a generalised linear model. RESULTS: 160 adults with type 2 diabetes (mean age 58.5 ± 11.5 years; BMI 33.7 ± 7.3 kg/m2; HbA1c 56.4 ± 14.3 mmol/mol) were randomised, with 143 (89%) providing end-of-intervention blood samples. HbA1c was lower following the less processed whole grain intervention compared with the more processed whole grain intervention (mean difference -2.2 mmol/mol, 95% CI -4.2, -0.1), despite no change observed in body weight between interventions. Whole grain, refined grain, and nutrient intakes did not differ between groups, with intervention foods providing approximately 20% of dietary energy. Among the secondary or exploratory outcomes, improvements were indicated only in self-reported bowel habits with less processed whole grains. CONCLUSIONS: Less processed whole grain foods were associated with improved glycated haemoglobin compared with more processed whole grain foods in adults with type 2 diabetes. These findings indicate that the degree of grain processing influences metabolic outcomes, support food reformulation, and distinguishing between refined grains, milled whole grains (wholemeal), and intact whole grains in dietary guidance, food marketing and labelling. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRY NUMBER AND WEBSITE WHERE IT WAS OBTAINED: ACTRN12622000060741.

articles.title: Almonds and the optimization of immune responses to influenza vaccination, compared to a control snack, in healthy adults: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Alice van der Schoot, Alice C Creedon, Noa Argomaniz et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Certain nutrient supplements enhance immune responses to vaccination; however, no randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have assessed the impact of a whole food. Almonds may benefit immune function through immunoregulatory nutrients and fiber, which interacts with the immune system via the gut microbiota. OBJECTIVE: This study assessed the effect of almonds on the immune response following influenza vaccination, compared to an isocaloric snack, in healthy adults. METHODS: In this RCT, healthy adults (40-64 years) consumed almonds (56 g/d) or an isocaloric control (86 g/d pretzels) for 8 weeks. Participants received seasonal influenza vaccine at week 4. The primary outcome was seroconversion rates for ≥1 strain at week 8. Antigen-specific antibody titers (HI assay) were quantified pre- (week 4) and post-vaccination (week 8), and seroconversion and seroprotection were calculated. The gut microbiota, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), stool output and gut symptoms were measured at baseline, midpoint and endpoint. RESULTS: Ninety participants were randomized (mean age 51 years, 73% females). Seroconversion rate for ≥1 strain was high and not significantly different between groups [almond: 38/41 (93%) versus control: 37/39 (95%), P=1.000], nor were strain-specific seroconversion or seroprotection rates. Almonds resulted in higher antibody titers for A/Wisconsin/67/2022 (H1N1) strain, compared to control [geometric mean (95% CI): almond 359 (146, 881) versus control 110 (51, 235)], and greater fold-change for A/Wisconsin/67/2022 (H1N1) [geometric mean fold change (95% CI): almond 18 (7, 48) versus control 4 (3, 7)] and B/Yamagata [almond 10 (6, 16) versus control 5 (3, 7)]. Absolute abundance of Roseburia hominis was significantly higher in the almond group compared to control (q=0.049). There was no effect on SCFAs or stool consistency. CONCLUSIONS: Almonds increased influenza vaccine antibody titers but did not affect seroconversion in a healthy population where vaccines are already highly effective. This trial was pre-registered at clinicaltrials.gov as NCT05515263 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05515263).

articles.title: Non-recurrent laryngeal nerve with dual branch pattern and merging: a rare anatomical variant encountered during right hemithyroidectomy.
articles.authors: Badriya Yussuf, Haissan Iftikhar
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The non-recurrent laryngeal nerve (NRLN) is an uncommon anatomical variant that passes directly from the vagus nerve to the larynx without the usual recurrent loop; it occurs on the right side in around one in a hundred individuals and is considerably rarer on the left. Its recognition is central to safe thyroid surgery, because an unanticipated NRLN lies in an unexpected position and is vulnerable to inadvertent injury. We report a right non-recurrent laryngeal nerve with an unusual dual-branch morphology in which the nerve divided and then re-merged before laryngeal entry. CASE PRESENTATION: A woman in her 50s underwent right hemithyroidectomy for a benign, compressive multinodular goitre of the right lobe. Intraoperatively, no recurrent laryngeal nerve was found in the expected tracheo-oesophageal groove; systematic tracing of the vagus nerve within the carotid sheath revealed a right NRLN that divided into a superior and an inferior branch. The two branches followed separate courses and re-merged into a single trunk approximately 10 mm before entering the larynx through the cricothyroid membrane. Both branches were identified and preserved. The patient was extubated uneventfully, demonstrated normal vocal cord function, and made an uncomplicated recovery with no voice change at early or later follow-up. CONCLUSION: Dual-branch NRLN in which the branches re-merge before laryngeal entry is a pattern we have not found previously described; while extra-laryngeal division of a non-recurrent nerve has been reported, the subsequent re-merging adds complexity to nerve identification and preservation. Awareness that a non-recurrent nerve may branch and re-merge should prompt complete tracing of every fascicle followed from the vagus during thyroid surgery.

articles.title: Suction-feeding performance in invasive alien giant salamanders within the functional framework of Andrias.
articles.authors: M López-Pachón, S Hayashi, J Fortuny et al.
articles.abstract: Hybridisation between Andrias japonicus and A. cf. davidianus lineages is a major conservation concern in Japan, but whether hybrid individuals retain the suction-feeding pattern described for non-hybrid Andrias remains unclear. We analysed suction feeding in six hybrid giant salamanders using 20 captive feeding events recorded with lateral and frontal high-speed videography. Skull, lower jaw, hyobranchial and prey movements were digitised to quantify trajectories, velocities and accelerations during the active expansion phase of prey capture. The hybrids displayed the characteristic suction-feeding sequence described for cryptobranchids, including mandibular opening, hyobranchial expansion, prey acceleration and capture once suction was initiated. Event-level variation occurred in relation to prey position, attack configuration and individual morphometrics, highlighting the flexibility of suction feeding performance among hybrid specimens. Overall, hybrid specimens retained suction-feeding kinematics within the functional pattern previously described for Andrias, suggesting that hybridisation does not disrupt the core biomechanical organisation of prey capture within the functional range examined here. When compared with published data for non-hybrid A. davidianus and A. japonicus, these results indicate a broadly conserved suction feeding mechanism rather than a distinct hybrid-specific feeding mode. Therefore, any potential ecological advantage of hybrids is unlikely to result from a fundamental change in the suction feeding sequence alone.

articles.title: Effect of Pain Science Education and Behavioral Graded Activity on Pain in Survivors of Breast Cancer: A Study Protocol for a Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.authors: Astrid Lahousse, Eva Roose, Laurence Leysen et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Pain affects up to half of survivors of breast cancer and is one of the most common long-term consequences of cancer treatment, yet it remains under-recognized and undertreated. Pharmacological options often provide limited relief and may cause adverse effects. Evidence from other pain populations supports a biopsychosocial approach combining pain education and physical activity. OBJECTIVE: The objective is to evaluate whether pain science education (PSE) with behavioral graded activity (BGA) versus usual care (UC), reduces pain intensity and interference in survivors of breast cancer with pain. Secondary aims include assessing health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and central pain modulation. DESIGN: This study is a multicenter, two-arm, assessor- and statistician-blinded, randomized controlled superiority trial. SETTING: The trial will be conducted in Belgium, with interventions delivered in hospital and academic research settings. PARTICIPANTS: Two hundred women with a history of breast cancer and persistent pain will be recruited. INTERVENTIONS: Participants will be randomized to either (1) PSE (1 session) plus 5 BGA sessions delivered by a trained physical therapist, or (2) usual care with a standardized biomedical pain information leaflet, over a 12-week period. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome will be pain intensity and interference (Brief Pain Inventory). Secondary outcomes will include HRQoL (EORTC QLQ-C30) and central pain modulation (Quantitative Sensory Testing). Exploratory outcomes include sleep, fatigue, pain-related cognitions, and health care utilization. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, post-intervention, and at 3-month (primary endpoint), 1-year, and 2-year follow-ups. CONCLUSIONS: This trial will determine whether a structured PSE+BGA program improves pain and HRQoL in survivors of breast cancer, offering a potential scalable non-pharmacological treatment. RELEVANCE: These findings may guide targeted rehabilitation strategies and strengthen the role of physical therapists in managing post-cancer pain, particularly in light of the growing population of survivors of breast cancer and the increasing prevalence of persistent symptoms.

articles.title: Critical appraisal of D3-creatine dilution method for skeletal muscle mass measurement.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Sri Lakshmi S Devarakonda, Carla M Prado, Steven B Heymsfield
articles.abstract: The D3-creatine dilution method is gaining rapid momentum as a tool for quantifying skeletal muscle mass (SMM), with emerging discourse positioning it as a reference standard and influencing peer-review and funding decisions. A critical appraisal of the method's current stage of development is therefore timely and necessary. We reviewed the current D3-creatine dilution method as now widely applied, its foundational assumptions, available validation studies comparing estimates against magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and sources of measurement error, including variability in the assumed skeletal muscle creatine concentration and isotope spillage correction. Only 4 studies with 102 total adult participants varying in sex (78 males), age, activity level (49 athletes), and health status have evaluated the current D3-creatine dilution SMM prediction model against MRI as the reference; mean group differences ranged from -13.8% to 20.9%, lending scant support for the validity of the current approach. The one longitudinal validation study (n = 14) reported wide limits of agreement, ±7 kg for D3-creatine compared with ±1.5 kg for MRI, raising concerns about the method's sensitivity to detect small changes in SMM. Isotope spillage correction algorithms, developed in 1 sample (n = 36), similarly require additional development and validation. Although D3-creatine dilution has potential as a new approach that can add to the multiple currently available SMM estimation methods, characterization as a reference standard for quantifying SMM is premature. Validation studies across well-defined cross-sectional and longitudinal samples varying widely in sex, age, diet, and health characteristics are needed to establish the D3-creatine dilution method's accuracy and generalizability.

articles.title: Use of Botanical Ingredients Relevant to Premenstrual Symptoms and Dysmenorrhea Among Elite Female Athletes: Evidence from Doping Control Forms.
articles.authors: Dominika Granda, Andrzej Pokrywka, Maria Karolina Szmidt et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and dysmenorrhea can impair training performance in female athletes. Botanical ingredients are commonly used to manage these conditions in the general population, but it is unknown whether elite female athletes do so. This study aimed to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea and determine whether elite female athletes declared them on Doping Control Forms (DCFs). METHODS: A narrative literature review was conducted to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea. Then, DCFs completed during routine anti-doping testing among elite athletes in Poland (2018-2023) were analyzed for declarations of these ingredients, both directly and as components of multi-ingredient products. The proportion of DCFs containing these ingredients was compared between female (n = 4451 DCFs) and male athletes (n = 9068 DCFs; reference) using chi-squared tests. RESULTS: The review identified 8 and 21 botanical ingredients with evidence for PMS and dysmenorrhea, respectively; of which 9 were detected in DCFs. The most commonly declared ingredients among female athletes were ginger and turmeric/curcuminoid (1.75% and 1.26%, respectively, both studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea). Chasteberry, on the other hand, with the most extensive, albeit low-confidence evidence, for PMS, was rarely declared (0.22%). Direct declaration of ginkgo, valerian, evening primrose oil, and chasteberry was significantly more common among female than male athletes (0.22% vs. 0.02%, 0.36% vs. 0.03%, 0.47% vs. 0.03%, 0.22% vs. 0.02%; adjusted p < 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: Declarations of botanical ingredients studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea were infrequent on DCFs completed by female athletes. Because DCFs do not record the reason for use, these data cannot establish whether declarations reflected treatment of menstrual symptoms; studies assessing indication, symptom status and motivation are needed.

articles.title: Comparing the coherent point drift algorithm to sliding semilandmark and weighted spherical harmonic whole-bone three-dimensional shape analyses.
articles.authors: Christine M Harper, Isabella F X Araiza, Deanna M Goldstein
articles.abstract: The ability to quantify 3D morphologies is critical for anatomical research; however, setting up high-density landmark sets and positioning them on all specimens can represent a substantial challenge. The coherent point drift (CPD) algorithm, a technique for registering two point clouds based on the Gaussian mixture model, was recently used to investigate human variation; however, its performance has yet to be compared to other 3D shape analysis methods. Here we compare the results of a CPD analysis to a sliding semilandmark and weighted spherical harmonic (SPHARM) analysis of the same 60 human and African ape calcanei and a CPD analysis and SPHARM-sliding analysis (a combination SPHARM and sliding semilandmark analysis) of 40 primate third manual proximal phalanges (mPP3s) to determine methodological comparability. Additionally, we run a CPD analysis on a small but wide-ranging sample of primate ulnae to demonstrate its utility for proximodistally long and mediolaterally narrow long bones. All specimens were surface or micro-CT scanned. All calcanei were subjected to a CPD analysis with 2000 semilandmarks, a sliding semilandmark analysis with 1007 semilandmarks, and a SPHARM analysis. All mPP3s underwent a CPD analysis with 2500 semilandmarks and a SPHARM-sliding analysis with 2562 semilandmarks. For the ulna, a CPD analysis with 1252 semilandmarks was run. Shape variation for all analyses was summarized using (separate) principal component analyses (PCAs). Results of the respective analyses for the calcaneus and mPP3 were compared by calculating the maximum and root mean square distances (RMSD) between average taxon shape configurations (scaled based on centroid size) generated from each analysis. All three calcaneus analyses separate taxa along the first two PCs, with humans separating from African apes along PC1 and chimpanzees and gorillas separating across PC2. For the two mPP3 analyses, the three great ape taxa consistently separate along PC1, and Papio separates from the other taxa along PC2. The average RMSD between CPD and sliding semilandmark analyses for the calcaneus was 0.24 mm, and 0.21 mm between CPD and SPHARM analyses. For the mPP3, the average RMSD between CPD and SPHARM-sliding was 0.14 mm. These results indicate that CPD is a comparable 3D shape analysis method to these other approaches. The CPD analysis was also able to place a semilandmark set on primate ulnae ranging from gorillas to tarsiers and capture morphological variations including shaft curvature, relative olecranon process length, and overall robusticity. CPD analyses are less time intensive than sliding semilandmark analyses; however, the sliding semilandmark analysis was better able to capture variation surrounding the borders of the articular facets (although differences were relatively minor), suggesting that these analyses may be better suited when the researcher is interested in a specific anatomical feature. CPD did capture edges better than SPHARM analyses; however, this is likely not an issue for small, relatively round bones such as carpals and most tarsals. In sum, CPD produces similar results to sliding semilandmark, SPHARM, and SPHARM-sliding approaches and has benefits for analyses of long bones with complex morphologies or among taxa that exhibit large amounts of morphological variation.

articles.title: Facial artery morphology assessed by computed tomography angiography: a mixed-effects morphometric analysis of age, sex, and laterality.
articles.authors: Sindy Melissa Sanchez-Romo, Adrian Manuel Verdines-Perez, Mario Campos-Coy et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The facial artery is the principal arterial supply to the midface and is among the most frequently encountered vascular structures during facial reconstructive, aesthetic, and minimally invasive procedures. Precise knowledge of its anatomical course and morphometric characteristics is essential to minimize vascular complications. However, previous morphometric studies have largely been descriptive and have rarely accounted for bilateral anatomical correlation or simultaneously evaluated the independent effects of age, sex, and laterality using appropriate multivariable statistical models. METHODS: A retrospective cross-sectional study was performed using computed tomography angiography (CTA) examinations from 103 adults, yielding 201 evaluable facial arteries. Standardized three-dimensional morphometric measurements were obtained at the inferior border of the mandible and the lateral alar base. Linear mixed-effects models incorporating patient-specific random intercepts were used to evaluate the effects of age, sex, side, and CTA diagnostic category while accounting for within-subject correlation. Measurement reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Bland-Altman analysis, and Cohen's kappa. RESULTS: Type III, according to the Furukawa classification, was the predominant anatomical pattern (67.2%). Among 98 patients with bilateral visualization, Furukawa type showed complete right-left concordance (100%; κ = 1.00). In an additional patient-level logistic model, neither age (OR 0.992 per year; 95% CI, 0.965-1.020; P = 0.584) nor female sex (OR 1.793; 95% CI, 0.767-4.191; P = 0.178) was significantly associated with Type III versus Type II. For continuous morphometric variables, no systematic laterality effect was detected, although individual-level bilateral agreement varied across parameters. After Holm correction across morphometric outcomes, women had a smaller facial artery diameter at the inferior border of the mandible and a shorter zygomatic arch-facial artery distance than men, while increasing age was independently associated with a shorter oral commissure-facial artery distance. Quantitative morphometric measurements demonstrated good-to-excellent observer reproducibility (intraobserver ICC: 0.900-0.960; interobserver ICC: 0.760-0.860), whereas categorical assessment of facial artery position relative to the nasolabial sulcus showed perfect intraobserver (κ = 1.00) and substantial interobserver agreement (κ = 0.79). CONCLUSIONS: CTA provides a reproducible morphometric assessment of the facial artery. No systematic laterality effect was identified for continuous morphometric variables, although individual bilateral agreement varied by measurement, while Furukawa type showed complete bilateral concordance in patients with both arteries visualized. Age and sex were not significantly associated with Furukawa Type III versus Type II, but they influenced selected continuous morphometric parameters. These findings characterize facial artery anatomy in a Mexican clinical cohort and may inform individualized anatomical assessment and preprocedural planning; they do not establish procedural risk thresholds.

articles.title: Regional Histological Anatomy of the Supraperiosteal Tissues of the Oral Cavity: Implications for Periodontal Flap Surgery and Periosteal Releasing Incisions.
articles.authors: Joe Iwanaga, Norio Kitagawa, Michitsuna Katafuchi et al.
articles.abstract: Periodontal and implant procedures increasingly involve tissue planes superficial to the periosteum, yet their regional anatomy remains poorly understood. This study conducted a histological investigation of the supraperiosteal anatomy of the oral cavity and its implications for periosteal releasing incisions (PRIs). Intraoral dissection of the mimetic muscle was performed using a fresh anatomical donor. Subsequently, maxillary and mandibular incisor, premolar, and molar regions from five formalin-fixed donors were examined histologically using Masson's trichrome staining. Muscular, neural, vascular, and connective tissue structures within 5 mm of the facial alveolar bone surface were evaluated. Supraperiosteal tissue architecture differed markedly by region. Muscular, neural, and vascular structures showed distinct region-specific distributions. The mental nerve and its branches were identified in the mandibular premolar region, whereas facial and buccal vessels were present near the bone surface in the posterior regions. Muscle attachment and intervening connective tissue also varied regionally. Structures potentially injured during PRI and their associated risks are region-dependent. PRI should therefore be guided by region-specific anatomy and the tissues requiring release for sufficient flap mobility rather than by a predetermined incision depth alone.

articles.title: Sex-specific Lower Limb Strength, Flexibility, and Running Biomechanics in Adolescents With and Without Osgood-Schlatter Disease.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Sungwan Kim, Alexandra F DeJong Lempke, Kristin E Whitney et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To examine sex-specific lower limb strength, flexibility, and running biomechanics in adolescents with and without OSD. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective chart review of 100 adolescents (n=25 each group): females with OSD (age=14.6 ± 1.9 y; body mass index [BMI]=21.3 ± 2.1 kg/m2); males with OSD (age=14.4 ± 1.6 y; BMI=21.7 ± 3.2 kg/m2); females without OSD (age=14.8 ± 2.2 y; BMI=21.7 ± 3.0 kg/m2); and males without OSD (age=14.4 ± 2.2 y; BMI=22.0 ± 4.6 kg/m2). We assessed mass-normalized sagittal and frontal hip strength and sagittal knee strength via hand-held dynamometry, and quadriceps femoris (prone knee flexion) and hip flexor (Thomas test) flexibility. Limb crossover, contralateral pelvic drop [CPD], medial knee displacement, and tibial dominant stride were assessed during treadmill running. Group differences were analyzed using a two-way multivariate analysis of variance (continuous outcomes) and logistic regression (categorical outcomes), covarying for age and BMI. Analyses were performed using SPSS (alpha set at p<0.05). RESULTS: Compared with sex-matched healthy peers, females with OSD had impaired hip abduction strength and a greater propensity for CPD and medial knee displacement, though greater hip flexion strength (p≤0.03; Table). Males with OSD had greater hip and knee sagittal plane strength yet impaired flexibility (p≤0.02; Table). Compared with males with OSD, females with OSD had lower hip and knee strength, greater quadriceps femoris flexibility, and higher odds of frontal plane biomechanical deficits (p≤0.02; Table). CONCLUSION: We observed sex-specific differences in lower limb muscular and biomechanical features in adolescents with OSD, suggesting that clinicians should consider sex-specific rehabilitation strategies for adolescents with OSD.

articles.title: Absorption and Metabolism of Steroidal Alkaloids from Tomato Juice in Healthy Adults: a Pharmacokinetic Study.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Daniel Do, Maria J Sholola, Jessica L Cooperstone
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Steroidal alkaloids may be responsible for some of the health benefits of a tomato rich diet, but little is known about their metabolic fate after consumption. OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to elucidate the pharmacokinetic parameters of plasma steroidal alkaloids and to define their bioavailability and metabolism following a single tomato containing meal. METHODS: Healthy subjects (n = 11, 6M/5F) consumed 505 g of tomato juice following a two-week tomato washout and blood plasma were collected post-prandially at 11 time points over 12-hours. Plasma steroidal alkaloids were analyzed using ultra-high performance liquid chromatography mass spectrometry. The pharmacokinetic parameters AUC0-12hr, Cmax, and Tmax were calculated using non-compartmental analysis. The quantity of steroidal alkaloids and their metabolites present in plasma were used to calculate a a fractional systemic exposure. Metabolite standards were "bio"-synthesized using the liver microsomes to improve confidence in identification when authentic standards were not available. RESULTS: The fraction of steroidal alkaloids from juice that appeared in plasma intact or as metabolized products was 9.7% ± 5.7% with a range of 2.4-17.9%. Over 99% of steroidal alkaloids present in circulation were metabolized products. The Cmax of total plasma steroidal alkaloids in subjects reached an average 406.5 nmol/L and ranged from 103.7-1145.6 nmol/L. Mean Tmax was 8.9 h (range 6-12 h) and average AUC0-12hr was 2529.0 ± 1644.8 nmol*h/L. Steroidal alkaloids remained above baseline at12 hours so absorption is likely underestimated. Liver S9 enzymatic synthesis of steroidal alkaloid metabolites including trihydroxy-tomatidine and sulfonated dihydroxy-tomatidine improved confidence in compound identification. CONCLUSIONS: This study reports the first pharmacokinetic data for tomato steroidal alkaloids, demonstrating moderate absorption and extensive metabolism after tomato juice consumption. These data provide context for future studies investigating the potential role that these compounds may play in human health. Clinical Trial Registry number and website where it was obtained https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01696773.
